items.title: You've probably seen it in the news:
items.subtitle: You've probably seen it in the news: some big AI model has over a hundred billion parameters.

items.title: So what actually is a parameter?
items.subtitle: So what actually is a parameter? And what does it mean to have that many?

items.title: Last time, we saw that today's AI mostly
items.subtitle: Last time, we saw that today's AI mostly figures out patterns on its own, from examples. What it ends up with is called a model.

items.title: So this time
items.subtitle: So this time, let's crack a model open and see what's really inside.

items.title: A model is basically a machine:
items.subtitle: A model is basically a machine: you feed an input in one end, and an answer comes out the other.

items.title: And on this machine
items.subtitle: And on this machine, there's a row of knobs. Turn them to different positions, and the same input gives a different answer.

items.title: Those knobs are the parameters.
items.subtitle: Those knobs are the parameters.

items.title: Here's an example:
items.subtitle: Here's an example: guessing a taxi fare. We put in the distance in kilometers, and out comes a guess at the price.

items.title: At its simplest
items.subtitle: At its simplest, this machine needs just two knobs: one for the base fare, and one for the price per kilometer.

items.title: To make a guess
items.subtitle: To make a guess, it multiplies the per-kilometer price by the distance, then adds the base fare.

items.title: Say the base fare is set to $10
items.subtitle: Say the base fare is set to $10 and the per-kilometer knob to $2. For a 5-kilometer ride, it guesses $20.

items.title: People decide how
items.subtitle: People decide how the machine does its math. But where each knob is set? Nobody types that in. The machine learns it from examples.

items.title: That's all "learning" is:
items.subtitle: That's all "learning" is: turning the knobs to the right positions.

items.title: Here are twelve made-up taxi rides.
items.subtitle: Here are twelve made-up taxi rides.

items.title: Each dot is one ride:
items.subtitle: Each dot is one ride: the further right, the longer the trip, and the higher up, the more it cost.

items.title: Put its guesses on a graph
items.subtitle: Put its guesses on a graph, and the straight line gives you a fare for any distance.

items.title: The little vertical line from each
items.subtitle: The little vertical line from each dot to that line shows how far off the guess was for that ride.

items.title: Let's start with the knobs
items.subtitle: Let's start with the knobs set pretty much at random: $0 base fare, $1 per kilometer. The line's way too low, and every ride gets underestimated.

items.title: Turn the base fare up to $10
items.subtitle: Turn the base fare up to $10, and the whole line lifts up.

items.title: Now the short rides are pretty close
items.subtitle: Now the short rides are pretty close, but the longer the ride, the further off it gets.

items.title: So turn the per-kilometer knob
items.subtitle: So turn the per-kilometer knob, and the line gets steeper. At $3.50 a kilometer, we've gone too far: now the long rides are overestimated.

items.title: Back the per-kilometer
items.subtitle: Back the per-kilometer knob off to about $2.50, and nudge the base fare up to $10.20.

items.title: Now the line runs right along the dots
items.subtitle: Now the line runs right along the dots, and all those little vertical lines are short.

items.title: Once it's tuned, you can actually use it.
items.subtitle: Once it's tuned, you can actually use it. So ask it: what would a ride of 8 kilometers cost?

items.title: None of our twelve rides
items.subtitle: None of our twelve rides was eight kilometers, but it can still make a guess: about $30.50.

items.title: So what did this machine actually learn?
items.subtitle: So what did this machine actually learn?

items.title: Everything it learned
items.subtitle: Everything it learned from those twelve rides comes down to where those two knobs are set.

items.title: The machine itself hasn't changed one bit.
items.subtitle: The machine itself hasn't changed one bit. Only the knob settings have.

items.title: Copy those two numbers
items.subtitle: Copy those two numbers onto a scrap of paper, hand it to a friend, and they've got the exact same model.

items.title: When people talk about "training a model,"
items.subtitle: When people talk about "training a model," all they're really doing is turning knobs.

items.title: Two knobs are plenty
items.subtitle: Two knobs are plenty for guessing a taxi fare. But if you want a model to write essays or chat with people, you need way, way more.

items.title: In 2020, OpenAI released GPT-3
items.subtitle: In 2020, OpenAI released GPT-3, which has 175 billion parameters.

items.title: That's a hundred
items.subtitle: That's a hundred and seventy-five billion knobs.

items.title: How many is that?
items.subtitle: How many is that? Read out one knob setting every second, no eating, no sleeping, and it'd take you over five and a half thousand years.

items.title: Obviously, nobody turned all those knobs by hand.
items.subtitle: Obviously, nobody turned all those knobs by hand. Their settings came from training on huge amounts of text.

items.title: But it's the same idea as the taxi fare:
items.subtitle: But it's the same idea as the taxi fare: people pick the math, and the settings are learned.

items.title: And a trained model, saved to a file
items.subtitle: And a trained model, saved to a file, is mostly just this long, long list of knob settings.

items.title: So when the news says "over
items.subtitle: So when the news says "over a hundred billion parameters," it means the machine has over a hundred billion knobs.

items.title: In short, a model is a machine with knobs.
items.subtitle: In short, a model is a machine with knobs.

items.title: And learning just means turning
items.subtitle: And learning just means turning the knobs to the right positions.

items.title: But what does "the right
items.subtitle: But what does "the right positions" actually mean?

items.title: Remember those little vertical lines
items.subtitle: Remember those little vertical lines, some long, some short? They're the clue.
